common_name: Clayton's Red Sunset Venus Flytrap (Deep Red Crescent-Trap Cultivar)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes or set out nursery starts into a moist, nutrient-poor mix of peat moss and perlite in full sun, watering only with rain or distilled water.

directions: Clayton's Red Sunset is a flytrap cultivar bred by Colin Clayton, selected for traps that take on an intense, almost purplish-red color under strong light, far deeper than the species default. The upright petioles carry traps with a distinctive arched, crescent-shaped profile and short, widely spaced marginal teeth rather than the longer interlocking spines of typical clones. Grow it exactly as any other Venus flytrap, in a saturated peat-and-perlite or pure sphagnum medium with only mineral-free water, and give it the brightest sun available to intensify the red coloring, since lower light causes it to green up. Provide a cool winter dormancy of a few months to maintain long-term vigor.
sources: ICPS Carnivorous Plant Newsletter Cultivar Descriptions

planting.note: Divide rhizomes into a constantly moist peat-and-perlite or pure sphagnum medium in full sun, using only rain or distilled water.

directions: Coquillage takes its name from the French word for shellfish, describing its traps' thickened, slightly cupped lobes with small, widely spaced marginal teeth that together suggest a pair of bivalve shells. The trap margins are notably smooth-edged compared to typical spiny-toothed flytraps, giving the whole structure a rounded, sculptural look. Culture is identical to any Venus flytrap: keep it standing in mineral-free water over a peat-perlite or sphagnum mix, give it strong direct sun, and allow a cool dormant rest in winter. It is a slower-growing, collector-oriented clone rather than a vigorous grower, so division for propagation is correspondingly slow.

common_name: Wrigley's Pitcher Plant (Natural Hybrid of Parrot Pitcher and White-Top Pitcher Plant)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes into a wet, nutrient-poor peat-and-perlite or sphagnum mix in full sun, standing the pot in a tray of rain or distilled water through the growing season.

directions: Sarracenia x wrigleyana is a naturally occurring cross between the low, decumbent S. psittacina and the tall, white-flushed S. leucophylla, found where the two species grow together in Gulf Coast savanna bogs. Plants show intermediate form, with pitchers more upright than psittacina but shorter and more flared at the hood than leucophylla, often marked with the same fine white netting on the upper pitcher. It combines leucophylla's striking color with some of psittacina's vigor and tolerance of wetter conditions. Grow it in full sun in a permanently saturated, acidic, mineral-free medium such as pure sphagnum or a peat-perlite blend, and allow a winter dormancy with cooler, reduced watering.

common_name: Pope's Pitcher Plant (Natural Hybrid of Yellow Pitcher Plant and Sweet Pitcher Plant)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes into a saturated, nutrient-poor peat-and-perlite or sphagnum mix in full sun, watering only with rain or distilled water.

directions: Sarracenia x popei arises naturally where S. flava and S. rubra grow side by side along the Gulf Coastal Plain, producing tall, slender pitchers that are intermediate in height and color between the two parents, typically yellow-green flushed with red veining toward the hood. The cross inherits flava's height and vigor along with some of rubra's narrower, more erect pitcher form and sweeter floral scent. It is winter dormant and needs a cold rest period to flower and pitcher well the following season. Grow in full sun in constantly wet, acidic, mineral-free medium, and divide congested clumps every few years in early spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Establish gemmae or divisions on the surface of a damp peat-and-sand or peat-perlite mix in bright, humid conditions, keeping the medium constantly moist with rain or distilled water.

directions: Drosera pygmaea is the most widely grown of the Australian and New Zealand pygmy sundews, forming a tiny flattened rosette of sticky, spoon-shaped leaves only a centimeter or so across. Unlike most pygmy Drosera it tolerates the same warm, humid, year-round growing conditions as tropical sundews, making it far easier to keep alive long-term than its more temperamental Western Australian relatives. It reproduces readily both by seed and by small plantlets called gemmae that form at the center of the rosette and can be sprinkled onto fresh damp substrate to start new plants. Keep the growing medium permanently wet, give it strong light to maintain compact growth and dew production, and expect individual rosettes to be short-lived but self-replacing through offsets and gemmae.

planting.note: Pot gemmae or offsets into a damp, sandy peat mix with excellent drainage and bright light, keeping it evenly moist but never waterlogged.

directions: Drosera scorpioides is a pygmy sundew from the forests and coastal heath of southwestern Australia, notably larger and shaggier than most of its relatives, with upright stems densely covered in long, reddish, glandular hairs that give the whole plant a fuzzy, almost woolly appearance. It is somewhat more tolerant of a brief dry or cool spell than other pygmy sundews but still prefers a sandy, well-drained peat mix rather than the saturated bog conditions suited to larger Drosera species. New plants are most reliably started from the small gemmae it produces at the growing point, which can be pressed onto fresh damp substrate. Give it bright light and consistent moisture, and protect it from hard frost since it has only modest cold tolerance compared with temperate sundew species.
